1128.title: Eat the fruit (Chagigah 15b)
1128.hook: Rabbi Meir found a pomegranate, ate the fruit and threw away the peel
1128.carry: eat the fruit, drop the peel
1128.howItsDone: Rabbi Meir's pomegranate is often cited in Jewish teaching when people discuss learning from mixed sources, along with the Talmud's caution that this takes maturity and discernment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Acher, the teacher who left, and your line: he kept walking with him. Today, the same page, one step further.

A pomegranate, split open. Red seeds packed tight, sweet and bright. Around them, a tough, bitter rind that nobody eats. Nobody throws away the fruit because of the peel, and nobody chews the peel because they like the fruit. The Talmud reaches for exactly this picture when it faces an uncomfortable question about Rabbi Meir and the teacher who left. Today, a fruit, a peel, and a surprising answer from heaven.
screen: `RED SEEDS, BITTER RIND.` → `AN UNCOMFORTABLE QUESTION.` → `AN ANSWER FROM HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday Rabbi Meir walked behind Acher and kept learning. Tractate Chagigah doesn't let that pass quietly. It asks: how could he? There's a teaching, built on a verse in the prophet Malachi, that you should learn Torah from a teacher only if he is like a messenger of the Lord: someone whose life matches his words. Acher's didn't. The Talmud answers in layers. First: a beginner should be careful, but someone grown in learning can tell what to keep and what to leave. And then a story. A sage named Rabbah bar Shila met the prophet Elijah and asked what the Holy One was doing. Elijah said: repeating teachings in the name of all the sages, except Rabbi Meir. Why not Meir? Because he learned from Acher. And Rabbah bar Shila objected: but Rabbi Meir found a pomegranate. He ate the fruit inside and threw away the peel. And Elijah said: now God says, Meir my son says. In the story, even heaven changes how it speaks. The picture is generous, and it's demanding. Generous, because it lets a person keep what is true and good from a teacher, a parent, a book or a place that also carried harm. Demanding, because you have to actually tell seed from rind, and the Talmud's own caution still stands: this is for the one who knows the difference. Not every source is safe for every learner at every stage. But the one who knows the difference isn't told to throw away the whole fruit.
screen: `HOW COULD MEIR LEARN FROM HIM?` · `FOR ONE WHO KNOWS THE DIFFERENCE.` · `HE ATE THE FRUIT, THREW THE PEEL.` · `MEIR MY SON SAYS.` · then, large: `EAT THE FRUIT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a source in your life that is mixed: a parent, a former teacher, a book you love that also has something ugly in it; if one hurt you deeply, choose a gentler one today. Name the peel honestly, without pretending it's all fruit. Then name one seed that is still good, still sweet, still yours, and hold it.
Eat the fruit. Rabbi Meir's way with the teacher who left: keep the fruit, throw away the peel, and know which is which. Today's word.
Your line: eat the fruit, drop the peel. Knowing which is which is the whole skill. See you tomorrow.

1129.title: How to begin
1129.hook: a teacher, a partner, and one line at a time
1129.howItsDone: Talmud is often studied with a chavruta, a study partner, reading aloud and debating each line, often under the guidance of a teacher in a yeshiva, synagogue class or online program.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pomegranate: keep the fruit, throw away the peel. Your line: eat the fruit, drop the peel. Today, a practical question.

A page of Talmud can look like a wall. Hebrew and Aramaic in the middle, commentaries crowding the margins, an argument already underway when you arrive, with names you don't know quoting verses you can't place. People open it, stare at it, and close it again. The tradition has an old answer for where to start, and it isn't a book or a course. It's two people, and a very small amount of text. Today: how to begin.
screen: `A PAGE LIKE A WALL.` → `WHERE DO YOU START?` → `TWO PEOPLE, A LITTLE TEXT.`

segments.voice: Pirkei Avot, in its first chapter, gives the advice of Yehoshua ben Perachiah: make for yourself a teacher, acquire for yourself a friend, and judge every person on the side of merit. A teacher and a friend. Not a library. The teacher is someone a little ahead of you on the road, who can say: this word means that, this question is coming, don't panic. The friend is a partner at your level. In study halls that partner is called a chavruta. Two people, one text, out loud. One reads a line and explains it; the other asks, but what about this? They argue. They check. They argue again. The Talmud praises this kind of learning with a verse from Proverbs: "Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend." And it warns from the other side, too: scholars who each sit alone to study, it says, grow foolish. Then, one line at a time. A mishnah is a few sentences. A sugya, one unit of argument, can be worked through slowly with a partner, then read again the next week, clearer. The way in isn't to master the whole thing. It's to find one person, sit across from them, and read one line slowly enough to disagree about it. Study halls, synagogues, community classes and online programs still pair learners this way. The form is old and simple: a teacher, a friend, a line.

1130.title: Block close: the sea
1130.hook: the Talmud is called a sea: no one crosses it, everyone can swim
1130.howItsDone: Jews learn Talmud in many ways: a daily page, a weekly class, a partner, a teacher, a single mishnah. At a siyum, learners often recite hadran, a promise to return to what they finished.

segments.voice: Yesterday, how to begin: a teacher, a friend, one line. Your line: one line with a partner. Today, the long block on the Mishnah and Talmud reaches the shore.

Some books get called a library. Some get called a mountain. The Talmud, in Jewish speech, is sometimes called a sea: yam haTalmud, the sea of Talmud. It's a picture of size and of depth, and of something else too. Nobody crosses a sea in an afternoon. Nobody drinks it dry. But you don't have to cross it to be in it. You only have to walk in from the beach.
screen: `A LIBRARY? A MOUNTAIN?` → `A SEA.` → `YOU DON'T HAVE TO CROSS IT.`

segments.voice: Look back along the shore we've walked. A written Torah, and an oral teaching beside it, written down when it might have been lost. The tannaim, who gave the Mishnah its words, and the amoraim, who discussed them line by line. The orders: seeds, appointed times, women, damages, holy things, purities. Then how the page works: a case and its voices, a sugya, a question left to stand, Rashi in the inner margin and Tosafot in the outer, the minority view kept for a later day. Then how law is decided: halakha, the way you walk, through the codes to questions about electricity and saving life. And these last days, living with it: a finished tractate, an open page, the ways of peace, hard passages, jokes, flawed heroes, a lost partner, a wounded sage, a teacher who left, and a pomegranate. Now the sea. The picture works three ways. No one crosses it. Even a siyum, the party for a finished tractate, ends with words that promise a return: hadran alakh, we will come back to you. Finishing isn't leaving. Everyone can swim. One mishnah, one line, one partner, and you're in the water; nobody checks your credentials at the beach. And the sea moves. Its currents are arguments that haven't stopped: Hillel and Shammai, a voice from heaven turned away, a question about a bird with one foot on each side of a line. You don't stand outside a sea and admire it. You get wet.
screen: `THE SHORE WE WALKED.` · `NO ONE CROSSES IT.` · `EVERYONE CAN SWIM.` · `THE SEA MOVES.` · then, large: `THE SEA OF TALMUD.`

1131.title: None like Moses
1131.hook: his epitaph says: from Moses to Moses there arose none like Moses
1131.howItsDone: Maimonides' works, especially the Mishneh Torah and the Guide for the Perplexed, are studied in yeshivas, universities and synagogue classes, and the saying 'from Moses to Moses there arose none like Moses' is often quoted in his honor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the block closed on the sea of Talmud, too wide to cross and open to anyone who wades in. Today, a new block, and one teacher.

Near its very end, the Torah stops to look back at Moses. After his death, it says, no prophet has arisen in Israel like him, whom the Lord knew face to face. Much later, Jews took that sentence and bent it, gently, to praise a second Moses. Tradition says the words came to be linked with his grave: from Moses to Moses, there arose none like Moses. Today begins a block about the man that saying praises.
screen: `THE TORAH'S LAST WORDS ON MOSES.` → `A SECOND MOSES.` → `FROM MOSES TO MOSES.`

segments.voice: Moses ben Maimon. In Hebrew he's usually called by an acronym, Rambam: Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon. In English, Maimonides. The saying plays on two men named Moses: from Moses the prophet to Moses ben Maimon, none arose like this Moses. It's praise, and it's a large claim. Notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't make him a prophet, and it doesn't put him above the first Moses. The verse in Deuteronomy reads, in the King James Bible, "there arose not a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses." The saying borrows the shape of that verse to honor a teacher. What did he teach? This block will walk through it. He wrote a commentary on the whole Mishnah. He wrote the Mishneh Torah, the code we met in the block just closed, setting out Jewish law in clear Hebrew, in one voice. He drew up principles of faith. He wrote the Guide for the Perplexed, for readers caught between Torah and philosophy. He worked as a physician, and wrote letters to communities in trouble. And not everyone welcomed him. His books stirred sharp arguments, in his own time and after; some communities embraced them and some opposed them, and that's part of his story too. So why say none like Moses? The saying ties him back to the first Moses, whom Jews call Moshe Rabbenu, Moses our teacher. It remembers Maimonides in that same line: not a lawgiver from the mountain, but a Moses who taught.

1132.title: Commentary on the Mishnah
1132.hook: written in Arabic while he was still young and wandering
1132.howItsDone: Students of the Mishnah often read Maimonides' commentary, in Hebrew translation, alongside the text; his introductions, such as the one to Pirkei Avot, are also studied on their own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, from Moses to Moses: a saying that honors Maimonides as a teacher. Today, the book where his own teaching began.

A long book, and at the very end of it, an apology. Maimonides closes one of his early books by asking the reader for patience. He wrote it, he says, while his mind was troubled and while he was on the move, some of it on the road and some of it at sea. So if you find a mistake, he asks, judge him kindly. Then look at what he had taken on while traveling: the Mishnah, the core text of the oral law, explained passage by passage. He says he wrote it while he was still young. Today, the book that started him.
screen: `AN APOLOGY AT THE END.` → `WRITTEN ON THE ROAD AND AT SEA.` → `THE MISHNAH, PASSAGE BY PASSAGE.`

segments.voice: Commentary on the Mishnah. In Hebrew, Perush HaMishnayot. First, the language. Maimonides wrote it in Arabic, the everyday language of the Jews around him, set down in Hebrew letters. He wanted it read and used, not admired. Hebrew translations came later, and those are what readers of the Hebrew page meet today. Second, the method. The Mishnah is terse. It often starts in the middle of an argument, as if you already know what the argument is about. Maimonides goes passage by passage and asks the beginner's questions. What is this about? What does this word mean? Which view is the law? Then he gives the bottom line, plainly. Third, the doorways. Before some sections he wrote long introductions that read like books of their own. One opens the whole Mishnah and explains how the oral tradition was handed down. One, on a chapter of tractate Sanhedrin, sets out the foundations of Jewish belief. One, before Pirkei Avot, is about the health of the soul. In the days ahead we'll walk through two of those doorways. Fourth, the ambition. A young man without a settled home decides to explain the whole Mishnah to ordinary readers, in their own language. And on the last page he asks forgiveness for his mistakes. Ambition and humility, bound into one book. Young and ambitious.

1133.title: The thirteen principles
1133.hook: his list of core Jewish beliefs, in his commentary on Sanhedrin 10
1133.howItsDone: Maimonides' thirteen principles are studied in his commentary on Sanhedrin, and versions of them appear in prayer books, both as the poem Yigdal and as a series of lines that each begin "I believe with complete faith."

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Commentary on the Mishnah, written on the road. Your line: young and ambitious. Today, one of its doorways.

All Israel have a share in the world to come. That, in paraphrase, is how a chapter of the Mishnah, in tractate Sanhedrin, opens. It backs the line with a verse from Isaiah: "Thy people also shall be all righteous." Then it names a few people who lose that share. The Mishnah stops there. It doesn't say what a share is, or what a person has to hold to keep one. Maimonides, working through the Mishnah passage by passage, reaches this chapter and decides the question can't wait. So he writes an answer, and the answer becomes a list.
screen: `A SHARE IN THE WORLD TO COME.` → `THE MISHNAH DOESN'T SAY WHAT IT IS.` → `MAIMONIDES WRITES A LIST.`

segments.voice: The thirteen principles. First, what he called them. Not commandments and not rules. In the Hebrew translation, they are yesodot, foundations, the stones a house stands on. You don't live in the foundation. You live in the house. But without it, the house doesn't stand. Second, the shape of the list. It moves in three stretches. The first five are about God. The next four are about prophecy and the Torah. The last four are about what God knows and does, and what is still to come. Over the next three days, we'll take one stretch a day. Third, why it was new. The Torah gives commandments. The Mishnah gives laws and arguments. Neither one stops to hand you a numbered list of beliefs. Maimonides did, in the middle of a commentary on the oral law, because he thought a person ought to know what the foundations are, not only what to do. Fourth, what came after. Later, his list was set in verse and printed in prayer books, and it was also questioned. Other scholars drew up lists of their own. That argument has a day of its own later this week. For now, notice the move. Faced with a single word in an old text, a share, Maimonides asked what it rests on, and wrote it down so that anyone could read it. Thirteen principles.
screen: `FOUNDATIONS, NOT RULES.` · `THREE STRETCHES: GOD, TORAH, WHAT'S TO COME.` · `A NUMBERED LIST OF BELIEFS.` · `READ, SUNG AND QUESTIONED.` · then, large: `THIRTEEN PRINCIPLES.`

segments.voice: Here is the list, plainly: God exists; God is one; God has no body; God is eternal; only God is to be worshiped; the prophets spoke truth; the prophecy of Moses stands apart; the Torah is from heaven; the Torah will not be replaced; God knows what people do; God rewards and punishes; the messiah will come; the dead will live. Hear it once without sorting it, and notice which line stays with you.
The thirteen principles. Maimonides' foundations of Jewish belief, set out in his commentary on the Mishnah's chapter about a share in the world to come. Today's word.
Your line: thirteen principles. A short list of what the whole house stands on. Rest well.

1134.title: Principles one to five
1134.hook: God exists, is one, has no body, is eternal, and alone is to be worshiped
1134.howItsDone: Jews say the Shema, "Hear, O Israel," in the morning and evening prayers and at bedtime; Maimonides' first principles are often taught alongside it, and his explanations of them are studied in his commentary and in the opening chapters of the Mishneh Torah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the thirteen principles: foundations, not rules. Your line: thirteen principles. Today, the first stretch, the one about God.

One what? It's a question a child might ask, and Maimonides takes it seriously. Behind it stands a line from Deuteronomy that Jewish prayer comes back to morning and night: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." His list builds on it, and takes up the child's questions one by one. One like a single apple is one? One like a team is one? And if the Torah talks about God's hand and God's eyes, does God have hands and eyes? His first five foundations are his answers. Today, the stretch of the list about God.
screen: `THE LORD IS ONE.` → `ONE LIKE WHAT?` → `FIVE FOUNDATIONS ABOUT GOD.`

segments.voice: Principles one to five. The first: God exists, and everything else exists because of God. Not the other way around. The world leans on God; God doesn't lean on the world. The second: God is one. And here Maimonides is careful. Not one like one of a pair, and not one like one member of a kind. Not one like a single body, which can still be cut into parts. A oneness, he says, unlike any other oneness. The third: God has no body. So what about the hand of God, the eyes of the LORD? He reads them as the Torah speaking in human language, so that people can understand. Deuteronomy reminds Israel that at Sinai they heard a voice but saw no form at all. The fourth: God is eternal. Before everything, after everything. In Isaiah's words: "I am the first, and I am the last." The fifth: only God is to be worshiped. Not the stars, not angels, not any power in between, as if God needed a go-between. Prayer goes straight to God. Now put them side by side. Each one takes something away. God isn't caused. God isn't many. God isn't a body. God doesn't begin or end. God doesn't need a messenger. Maimonides teaches God, here, mostly by saying what God is not. One, bodiless, eternal.
screen: `GOD EXISTS, AND ALL ELSE LEANS ON GOD.` · `ONE, UNLIKE ANY OTHER ONE.` · `NO BODY, NO FORM.` · `ETERNAL, AND WORSHIPED ALONE.` · then, large: `ONE, BODILESS, ETERNAL.`

segments.voice: Let the word one arrive on the in-breath, and let it go on the out-breath. When a picture comes with it, a number, a shape, a face, let it pass; Maimonides kept taking pictures away. If you pray, you can say the line from Deuteronomy once, quietly.
Principles one to five. The first stretch of Maimonides' list: God exists, is one, has no body, is eternal, and alone is to be worshiped. Today's word.
Your line: one, bodiless, eternal. No picture is big enough, so he kept setting them down. See you tomorrow.
